name: @rndmjoker/proton-mcp

tools.name: check_for_updates
tools.description: Asks the npm registry whether a newer version of this server exists, and reports how to install it. **This is the only thing in this server that connects to anything other than the Proton Mail Bridge on this machine**, so call it when the user asks about updates rather than by habit, and say that it means one request to registry.npmjs.org. It sends nothing about the user or their mail, and it installs nothing: updating is left to the person, deliberately.

tools.name: list_folders
tools.description: Lists the folders and labels of the Proton account. Proton distinguishes folders (a message lives in exactly one) from labels (a message can carry any number). Over IMAP both appear as directories.

kind.description: Which mailboxes to list. "system" covers Inbox, Sent, Trash and so on, "folder" the user-created folders, "label" the labels.

onlySelectable.description: When true, only mailboxes that can hold messages are listed.

tools.name: list_messages
tools.description: Lists the messages of a mailbox, newest first by the date the sender wrote, which also holds across pages. Returns headers only: sender, subject, date, size and the message id. It never returns message bodies, because a single message averages around 16000 tokens raw. Use get_message with an id to read one. Ordering reads one date per message in the mailbox, so a very large mailbox takes a moment; the answer says so when it does.

mailbox.description: The mailbox path, for example "INBOX", "Archive" or "Folders/Work". Use list_folders to see them. "All Mail" holds every message including discarded ones, and there the entries that are in the trash come back marked "in trash".

limit.description: How many messages to return, at most 100.

offset.description: How many of the newest messages to skip. Used for paging.

unreadOnly.description: When true, only unread messages are listed.

tools.name: search_messages
tools.description: Searches a mailbox by text, subject, sender, recipient, date range, read state, star or size. At least one criterion is required. Returns headers only, newest first across pages, with paging. A full-text search walks the local database of the Bridge and takes a few seconds on a large mailbox, while criteria such as unread or date are fast. Searching "All Mail" covers every mailbox including trash, and entries that are in the trash are marked "in trash" - the other marks are flags rather than places, so "draft" says a message is one, not that it is in Drafts.

mailbox.description: Which mailbox to search. Defaults to "All Mail", which holds every message, discarded ones included. Those come back marked "in trash".

text.description: Free text, matched against body and headers. This is the slow criterion.

from.description: Substring of the sender address or display name.

since.description: Only messages the sender dated on or after this day, as YYYY-MM-DD. Compared against the Date header, which is what the results show.

before.description: Only messages the sender dated before this day, as YYYY-MM-DD. Compared against the Date header, which is what the results show.

unreadOnly.description: When true, only unread messages. False and omitted both mean no filter.

starredOnly.description: When true, only starred messages. False and omitted both mean no filter.

largerThan.description: Minimum size in bytes. Useful for finding messages with large attachments.

offset.description: How many results to skip, for paging.

tools.name: get_message
tools.description: Reads one message by its id and returns it as readable text. HTML is converted to text, images and styling are dropped and no external content is fetched. Long bodies are shortened with a visible note. The body is marked as untrusted third-party content.

messageId.description: The message id from list_messages or search, passed on unchanged.

mailbox.description: Optional: the mailbox to look in first. Saves a lookup. Without it the search goes through "All Mail".

maxChars.description: Optional character budget for the body. Higher values cost context.

textOffset.description: Where to continue reading a long message. The answer names the next offset when something was left out, so a long message can be read in parts instead of raising the budget until it fits.

tools.name: get_attachment
tools.description: Reads one attachment of a message by index. The index comes from the attachment list in get_message. Textual attachments are returned as text, binary ones are refused with a reason rather than dumped into the context.

messageId.description: The message id the attachment belongs to.

index.description: Index of the attachment, as shown by get_message. Starts at 0.

mailbox.description: Optional: the mailbox to look in first.

offset.description: Where to continue reading a long attachment. The answer names the next offset.

tools.name: add_label
tools.description: Applies an existing label to a message. In Proton a message lives in exactly one folder but can carry any number of labels, so this adds to the message rather than moving it: it stays where it is and keeps the labels it already has. The label has to exist already; this server does not create labels.

messageId.description: The message id from a listing or a search, with or without angle brackets.

label.description: The label name, for example "Work". The "Labels/" prefix may be included and is optional. Use list_folders to see which labels exist. Labels are created in Proton itself, not here.

mailbox.description: The mailbox the message is in, if known. Only a shortcut for the lookup.

tools.name: remove_label
tools.description: Removes a label from a message. The message keeps its folder and its other labels, and does not go to trash. Only labels can be removed this way, never folders: a message always lives in some folder, and moving it is a different operation.

messageId.description: The message id from a listing or a search, with or without angle brackets.

label.description: The label name, for example "Work". The "Labels/" prefix may be included and is optional. Use list_folders to see which labels exist. Labels are created in Proton itself, not here.

tools.name: move_messages
tools.description: Moves messages into a folder. In Proton a message lives in exactly one folder, so this takes it out of the one it is in. Labels are not affected and survive the move. Only folders are valid destinations: moving into a label would apply the label and leave the message where it is, so a label is refused here and add_label does that job. The destination has to exist; this server does not create folders.

messageIds.description: The message ids, as they came from a listing or a search. At most 50 per call.

target.description: The destination folder, for example "Archive" or "Folders/Work". Use list_folders to see the paths. Note that Proton fills the inbox through delivery: a message moved to "INBOX" over IMAP was measured to end up elsewhere shortly afterwards.

mailbox.description: The mailbox the messages are in, if they share one. Only a shortcut: without it every message is looked for across the mailboxes it could be in, which costs a request each.

tools.name: set_flags
tools.description: Marks messages as read or unread and sets or clears the star. At least one of the two has to be given. This changes nothing about where a message sits and nothing about its content. Proton shows the star as the "Starred" mailbox.

messageIds.description: The message ids, as they came from a listing or a search. At most 50 per call.

read.description: True marks the messages as read, false as unread. Omit to leave it alone.

starred.description: True stars the messages, false removes the star. Omit to leave it alone.

mailbox.description: The mailbox the messages are in, if they share one. Only a shortcut: without it every message is looked for across the mailboxes it could be in, which costs a request each.

tools.name: trash_messages
tools.description: Moves messages to the trash. This is what deletion means here: the messages stay in "Trash" and in "All Mail" and can be moved back out with move_messages. There is no tool in this server that deletes a message for good or empties the trash, so that a wrong decision stays reversible.

messageIds.description: The message ids, as they came from a listing or a search. At most 50 per call.

mailbox.description: The mailbox the messages are in, if they share one. Only a shortcut: without it every message is looked for across the mailboxes it could be in, which costs a request each.

tools.name: create_draft
tools.description: Writes a new draft into the Drafts mailbox. Nothing is sent. Attachments from files on this machine are not supported on purpose. The body is plain text and markup is not interpreted. HTML written here is delivered as visible characters, so the recipient would read the tags rather than see formatting. Give a message its shape with line breaks, blank lines, indentation and plain lists, and write a link as the bare address so that what is read is what is followed. A message may instead be written as markup, in the html field, which is delivered as formatting rather than as visible tags. Give one or the other, not both: a message that carries markup has its plain text half dropped, so the half that was confirmed would never arrive. Permitted are headings, paragraphs, line breaks, rules, quotes, emphasis, lists, tables, links and images, with colour, font, alignment, spacing and borders. Anything else is refused rather than quietly removed, and the answer names what and why. Note that the preview page linked from the confirmation lists every address in the message in full, including the ones behind links and images, and every alt text, because those are what a recipient reads. The question in the client stays short and carries counts instead. Text is UTF-8 everywhere: subject, body and addresses. Write characters as the language actually spells them, including umlauts, accents, sharp s, quotation marks and any other non-ASCII character. Do not transliterate them away (no "ae" for "ä", no "ss" for "ß"): the subject is encoded for transport and decoded again on arrival, and the body carries its character set, both verified against the Bridge. A transliterated message is simply a message with the wrong words in it.

to.description: The main recipients. Each entry is an address, optionally as "Display Name <name@example.com>".

cc.description: Recipients in copy, visible to everyone. Each entry is an address, optionally as "Display Name <name@example.com>".

bcc.description: Recipients in blind copy, hidden from the others but they do receive it. Each entry is an address, optionally as "Display Name <name@example.com>".

html.description: The body as markup instead of plain text. Give this or text, not both. Permitted are headings, paragraphs, line breaks, rules, quotes, emphasis, lists, tables, links and images, with colour, font, alignment, spacing and borders. Images may point at a full address; anything outside the permitted set is refused with a reason rather than removed.

markupLevel.description: How much markup is permitted. "standard" covers ordinary formatted mail. "extended" permits every CSS property, including ones that can hide content, and makes the confirmation carry a warning telling the person to open the preview. Prefer "standard"; reach for "extended" only when asked for something that needs it, such as a button, which requires display:inline-block.

tools.name: reply_draft
tools.description: Writes a reply to a message as a draft. The recipient is the message's Reply-To if it set one, otherwise its sender. The original is quoted below the new text. Nothing is sent. Note on threading: the reply is built with In-Reply-To and References, but Proton replaces those with its own internal thread id when it stores a draft, so a draft that is stored and sent later carries Proton's idea of the conversation rather than ours. The body is plain text and markup is not interpreted. HTML written here is delivered as visible characters, so the recipient would read the tags rather than see formatting. A transliterated message is simply a message with the wrong words in it.

messageId.description: The message id from a listing or a search, with or without angle brackets.

text.description: The reply itself. The original is quoted below it.

replyAll.description: When true, the other recipients of the original are put in copy.

html.description: Your part of the message as markup instead of plain text. The original is quoted below it either way. The quote keeps the original's own markup, character for character, minus what would reach out of it: style blocks, document-level elements, scripts and comments. A message this server would not itself compose can therefore still be replied to or forwarded, but its formatting travels along, and so does anything a link in it points at.

tools.name: open_configuration
tools.description: Returns the address of the local configuration interface, which runs for as long as this server does and is where everything about this server can be seen and changed. Give it to the user whenever they ask for the interface, the panel, the settings, the web page, the address or the link, however they phrase it, and also when they ask where to sign in, where to see what has been sent, where the folders are listed, or when another tool reports that no credentials are available. The address contains an access token and changes every time the server restarts, so it cannot be remembered from an earlier conversation and has to be asked for again.

instructions:
This server reads and writes a Proton Mail account through a local Proton Mail Bridge.

Four things are worth knowing before the first call, because they are the ones that go
wrong quietly:

1. Nothing is sent without a person agreeing to it. Every sending tool asks first, through
   the client, showing the final recipients. The first call never sends, and there is no
   setting that turns the question off.
2. A message body is either plain text or markup, never both. Markup written into the text
   field arrives as visible tags. All text is UTF-8: write words the way the language
   spells them rather than transliterating characters away.
3. Writes need time to settle, and how much depends on what was written. Flags are
   immediate; a move takes about fifteen seconds; a new message needs about twenty before
   it appears in "All Mail". Checking straight after a write reports an intermediate state
   as though it were the result.
4. Nothing here deletes for good. "Delete" means moving to the trash.

Everything about this server is seen and changed in a local page, and open_configuration
returns its address. Hand that address over whenever it is asked for, in whatever words: it
carries an access token, changes on every restart, and cannot be guessed or remembered.

Two guides can be read when they are needed:
  proton-mcp://guide/writing   composing messages, formatting, quoting, what the
                               confirmation shows
  proton-mcp://guide/bridge    how the Bridge behaves, with the measurements behind the
                               numbers above
